painBullets: A risk list is a snapshot. It shows what is open now but not whether the count and severity are falling over time.
Risks marked mitigated are not always retired in the work, so the burndown looks better than the project actually is.
New risk arrives as fast as old risk is closed, and without a trend that churn is invisible until the date is at hand.

Risk inflow is easy to miss. A flat count can hide steady churn, where every retired risk is replaced by a new one nobody flagged.

primaryPain: At program scope, the risk that matters is rarely visible from any one project. Each workstream reports its own status, but the program level exposure, where two projects share a dependency, where a slip in one cascades into three others, lives in the space between them. Assembling that picture by hand means waiting for every project to report, then reconciling versions that already disagree, and by then the program view is a week behind the program.
painBullets: Each project reports its own risk, so the program dashboard is only as current and as honest as the slowest workstream.
Risks that cross projects, a shared dependency or a cascading slip, have no owner and appear on no single project's board.
Rolling up risk by hand means reconciling reports that disagree, so the program view is stale before it is even assembled.
whyHardHeading: Why program scope is harder than project scope
whyHard: A program is not a bigger project. Its worst risks are the interactions between workstreams, which no single project board is built to show.
Each project holds one fragment of the truth, and the program view requires reconciling all of them, which is exactly the work that lags.
The more workstreams a program runs, the more seams exist between them, so the surface where program level risk hides grows with every team added.
howHusnHelps: Husn reads Jira, Slack, and your docs across every workstream and rolls risk up to program scope automatically, so the dashboard reflects the whole program, not the slowest report.
It identifies risks from tickets, threads, and updates as they form and flags the ones that cross projects, where a slip in one cascades into others.
